markup: Text fields use a small markup that scripts/build-students.mjs renders: [text](url) for links, **text** for bold lead-ins, {{refId}} for a numbered citation to refs.refId, [[role:slug]] for a link to a Pathway Finder role guide. Blocks: p, ul, ol, note, warn, h3, table {caption, head, rows}, cards (the guide's own page list).

pages.title: Plan your cybersecurity degree, year by year
pages.metaTitle: CCAIR Student Guide: A Year-by-Year Cybersecurity Plan
pages.desc: A free, sourced plan for cybersecurity students: what to do in your first month, each semester, each year and your final year, from the Center for CyberAI Research.
pages.summary: A year-by-year plan: first month, every semester, every year and your final year.
pages.lede: This guide turns the advice we give Center for CyberAI Research (CCAIR) students into a plan you can follow. Dates, prices and rules change often, so every one of them links to the public source we checked.

ol: **Pick two or three target work roles.** The NICE Workforce Framework (the common language for cybersecurity jobs, maintained by the National Institute of Standards and Technology) lists 42 work roles in 5 categories{{niccs-nice}}. The [Pathway Finder](/ccair/pathways/) narrows them down in about five minutes.
**Find a faculty mentor.** Agree on a meeting schedule at the first meeting, and keep it.
**Start a resume.** If federal work is a goal, create a USAJOBS profile now as well{{usajobs}}. See [Get hired](/ccair/students/get-hired/).

**Start a records file for a future security clearance.** The clearance questionnaire asks for 10 years of addresses, employers and schools, and 7 years of foreign travel and close foreign contacts{{sf86}}. Write each one down as it happens. See [Security clearances](/ccair/students/security-clearance/).
**Learn research ethics basics.** Complete your campus research ethics training before you work with data about people{{ohrp}}.

ul: **Keep your grades up.** For many federal technical jobs, a 3.0 grade point average (GPA) overall or 3.5 in your major is one way to qualify for a higher starting grade (Superior Academic Achievement){{opm-gsqp}}.
**Take one skill step.** Finish a competition, a course or a certification step each term. See [Build skills](/ccair/students/skills/) and [Certifications](/ccair/students/certifications/).
**Meet your mentor on schedule.** Bring a short written update and one specific question.

**Fall: apply for next summer's internships.** Many internships close months before summer starts, so check each posting's closing date. Federal student internships (the Pathways Internship Program) are posted on USAJOBS{{opm-pathways}}.
**Summer: work in a security role.** An internship, a research assistantship or a campus IT security job gives you experience to describe on a resume.
**Spring: update your plan.** Compare your resume with two real job postings for your target role and close one gap before fall.
**Apply broadly.** Use USAJOBS, agency career sites and private employers at the same time.
**Use the Pathways Recent Graduates Program.** You must apply within two years of finishing your degree (up to six years for some veterans){{opm-pathways}}.
**Expect paperwork if the job needs a clearance.** Your records file turns a stressful form into a copying exercise.

blocks.p: Having a plan matters less than following it. The pages below cover each step in detail.

pages.title: Build skills with free training, practice and competitions
pages.metaTitle: Free Cybersecurity Training, Practice and Competitions for Students
pages.desc: Where cybersecurity students can train for free, practice hands-on and compete, organized around the NIST NICE Framework work roles.
pages.summary: Free training, hands-on practice and competitions, organized by work role.
pages.lede: Employers hire for evidence that you can do the work. Free training gives you the concepts, practice platforms give you the hands-on time, and competitions give you results you can list.

blocks.p: The NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity is at version 2.2.0 of its components, released April 28, 2026{{nice-news}}. It lists 42 work roles in 5 categories and 11 competency areas, including Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security{{niccs-nice}}{{niccs-comp}}. Pick a role first, then choose training that builds its skills.

table.caption: Seven common NICE work roles and the matching Pathway Finder guide
head: NICE work role
ID
Role guide

blocks.p: The role IDs come from the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Careers and Studies (NICCS) framework tool{{niccs-nice}}.

ul: **CISA Learning.** The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) replaced its old FedVTE platform with CISA Learning. It offers about 850 hours of no-cost training mapped to the NICE Framework, and U.S. residents sign in with Login.gov{{cisa-learning}}.
**NICCS Education and Training Catalog.** A searchable list of thousands of in-person and online cybersecurity courses from many providers{{niccs-catalog}}. Check the price on each listing.

**MITRE ATT&CK training.** MITRE publishes courses on ATT&CK (a public knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques), including ATT&CK Fundamentals and a Cyber Threat Intelligence course{{attack-training}}.
**Microsoft Learn AI security fundamentals.** A beginner learning path of three modules: AI security, AI security controls and an introduction to AI security testing{{ms-ai-sec}}.
**OverTheWire.** Start with Bandit, which teaches Unix and Linux basics through short levels{{otw}}.
**CyLab Security Academy.** Carnegie Mellon's free practice platform, formerly picoCTF. Older picoCTF logins still work{{cylab}}.
**TryHackMe.** Guided exercises that run in your browser. Students get 20% off an annual Premium subscription{{thm}}.
**Hack The Box Academy.** A discounted student subscription is available once you verify an academic email address{{htb}}.
**After graduation: SANS Cyber Academy.** Free, intensive training for career changers. Full-time students are not eligible, and it requires U.S. citizenship or permanent residence{{sans}}.
**National Cyber League (NCL).** Individual and team games run each fall and spring. High school and college students in the United States and Canada can play{{ncl}}.

**Collegiate Cyber Defense Competition (CCDC).** College teams run and defend a business network against a live attacking team, through regional rounds to a national final{{ccdc}}. Ask your department whether it fields a team.

blocks.p: Competitions give you a rank, a date and a team to describe in an interview. One season of NCL is a reasonable first goal.

ul: **Keep a log.** Record what you solved, the tool you used and what you learned, with the date.
**Write one short write-up a month.** Explain a solved challenge in plain language (after the competition ends, never during it).
**Link it from your resume.** A hiring manager can read one page of your work in two minutes.

pages.title: Certifications: which to take, and when
pages.metaTitle: Cybersecurity Certifications for Students: Which and When
pages.desc: Which cybersecurity certifications students should take first, which to leave for later, current exam versions, student discounts and DoD 8140 rules.
pages.summary: Which certifications to take first, current exam versions, discounts and DoD 8140.
pages.lede: Most students need one entry certification before their first job. Leave advanced ones until you have the experience they require, and check the exam version before you buy study materials.

sections.h: Start with the job, not the certificate

blocks.p: Pick your target role first. Each [Pathway Finder role guide](/ccair/pathways/#roles) lists its starter and later certifications. Then use the tables below to check the current exam and the dates that affect you.

table.caption: Entry certifications, current exams and key dates (checked October 2026)
head: Certification
Exam
Date or price to know

blocks.p: Pick one Security+ version and study only for it. SY0-701 stays available in English until June 11, 2027, and SY0-801 adds objectives on risks in AI systems, models, prompts and data exposure{{secplus-v8}}.
ISC2 ended its free One Million Certified in Cybersecurity program on May 20, 2026. If you hold an unexpired free code, you must take the exam by December 31, 2026{{isc2-1mcc}}.
CySA+ suits security operations center (SOC) and vulnerability analyst roles, and CompTIA recommends about four years of experience in them{{cysa-v4}}. Treat it as a second certification.

table.caption: Advanced certifications and what they need
head: Certification
What it needs
rows: 3 to 4 years in IT, 2+ in security, recommended{{secai}}

blocks.p: You can pass the Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) exam before you have the experience and become an Associate of ISC2. You then have six years to earn the five years of experience. A degree in computer science, IT or a related field can count for one year, and paid or unpaid internships count as experience{{cissp-exp}}.
Microsoft's SC-500 exam leads to the Cloud and AI Security Engineer Associate credential{{ms-sc500}}. AWS has used exam SCS-C03 since December 2, 2025{{aws-scs-doc}}.

ul: **CompTIA.** Verify your student status through SheerID to get academic pricing{{comptia-student}}.
**ISC2 Candidate.** The first year is free, then US$50 a year. It includes 10% off ISC2's official online self-paced training{{isc2-candidate}}.
**ISACA.** Student membership is US$25 a year plus local chapter dues{{isaca}}.

blocks.p: Ask your department about vouchers before you pay full price.

sections.h: If you want to work for the Department of Defense

blocks.p: Department of Defense (DoD) Manual 8140.03 took effect on February 15, 2023 and cancelled the old DoD 8570.01-M{{dodm-8140}}. Positions are coded to work roles in the DoD Cyber Workforce Framework (DCWF). You meet foundational qualification through education, training or a personnel certification within 9 months of assignment, and resident (on-the-job) qualification within 12 months{{dodm-8140}}{{cwm-8140}}.

Security+ was one of the first certifications approved under DoD 8140{{comptia-8140}}. However, not every certification counts for every work role. Check the DoD 8140 qualification matrix for your target work role before you buy a voucher{{cwm-matrix}}.

pages.title: Get hired in the private sector or federal government
pages.metaTitle: How Cybersecurity Students Get Hired: Private and Federal Jobs
pages.desc: Resumes, federal job announcements, OPM's Merit Hiring Plan, GS grades and series, structured interviews and where to find cybersecurity jobs.
pages.summary: Resumes, federal announcements, assessments, GS grades and where to look.
pages.lede: Private and federal employers want the same evidence: what you did, with what result. Federal applications add strict format rules and formal assessments, so read this page before you apply on USAJOBS.

sections.h: Write one strong resume, then tailor it

ul: **Lead with evidence.** Use numbers: labs completed, competition ranks, systems you supported, hours per week.
**Use the posting's language.** Repeat the announcement's words for skills you actually have.
**List certifications with dates.** Include one in progress with your target exam date.
**List education with your GPA** if it helps you (see grades below).

**Two pages at most.** Since September 27, 2025, USAJOBS limits resumes to two pages for Title 5 competitive and excepted service announcements. A longer resume makes you ineligible for that announcement{{opm-2page}}.
**Complete job entries.** For each job, list the title, the employer (with series and grade for federal jobs), start and end dates by month and year, and hours worked per week{{opm-2page}}.
**Leave out personal data.** Do not include your Social Security Number, photos, age, sex, religious affiliation or any classified information{{usajobs-leave}}.

sections.h: Read a federal announcement in four places

ol: **This job is open to.** Confirms which applicants are eligible, such as recent graduates or the public.
**Qualifications.** The specialized experience or competencies your resume must show.
**How you will be evaluated.** Names the assessments, such as USA Hire tests, work samples or structured interviews.
**Required documents.** A missing transcript can end an application.

blocks.p: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) Merit Hiring Plan of May 2025 requires at least one technical or alternative assessment before a list of candidates goes to the hiring manager. Self-rating questionnaires can no longer be used to rank applicants{{opm-mhp}}.

Announcements at GS-5 and above include short essay questions. OPM says answers are not scored or rated, and skipping them does not screen you out{{opm-essay}}. If you answer, stay under 200 words per question and use your own words: you certify that you did not use a consultant or AI{{opm-mhp}}. On September 11, 2026, a federal court stayed use of the third question, and OPM replaced it for announcements opening on or after September 19, 2026{{opm-stay}}.

Structured interviews ask every candidate the same questions. OPM recommends the STAR method (Situation or Task, Action, Result) for these questions{{opm-star}}. Prepare six to eight STAR stories, each tied to a competency in the announcement.

table.caption: Federal job series common in cybersecurity
head: Series
Name

blocks.p: IT Cybersecurity Specialist is one of the basic titles in the 2210 series{{opm-2210-titles}}.

For most technical series, education sets your starting grade. A bachelor's degree qualifies for GS-5. Superior Academic Achievement or one year of graduate study qualifies for GS-7, a master's degree for GS-9 and a PhD for GS-11{{opm-gsqp}}. Superior Academic Achievement means the upper third of your class, a GPA of 3.0 overall or 3.5 in your major, or membership in a national scholastic honor society{{opm-gsqp}}.

However, the 2210 series changed in April 2026. OPM's new competency-based standard says education cannot be used in place of the required competencies, and agencies must also use an assessment{{opm-2210-memo}}{{opm-2210-std}}. For 2210 jobs, show the competencies through projects, labs and work.

Series 0854, 1550 and 2210 have a special salary table (999B) at GS-5, 7, 9 and 11 in many locations. You are paid the special rate or your locality rate, whichever is higher{{opm-999b}}. Check OPM's current tables for your city before you compare offers{{opm-pay}}.

ul: **USAJOBS.** Nearly every federal civilian job{{usajobs}}.
**Pathways Programs.** The Internship Program (enrolled at least part-time) and the Recent Graduates Program (within two years of your degree){{opm-pathways}}.
**IntelligenceCareers.gov.** Jobs and student programs across the Intelligence Community{{ic-careers}}.
**DHS Cybersecurity Service.** The Department of Homeland Security's own cyber hiring system{{dhs-cs}}.
**CISA careers.** Jobs and student opportunities at CISA{{cisa-careers}}.
**US Tech Force.** Two-year federal terms that mainly recruit early-career technologists, including in cybersecurity{{techforce}}.
**State, local and private employers.** CyberSeek maps cybersecurity job demand by state and metro area{{cyberseek}}.

pages.title: Security clearances: start preparing now
pages.metaTitle: Security Clearances for Students: How It Works and What to Do Now
pages.desc: How a US security clearance works, the 13 adjudicative guidelines, and what students should do now about honesty, drugs, finances and records. General information, not legal advice.
pages.summary: How the process works, the 13 guidelines and what to do now.
pages.lede: Many federal and defense cybersecurity jobs require a clearance. You cannot apply for one yourself, but the choices you make as a student shape how the process goes.
pages.disclaimer: General information, not legal advice. Rules differ by agency and change over time. For your own situation, ask the hiring agency's security office or a qualified attorney.

ol: **A job offer.** The employer or agency sponsors your clearance after a tentative offer.

**The questionnaire.** You complete the SF-86 (Questionnaire for National Security Positions) in NBIS eApp, the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) system{{isl-eapp}}. The government is replacing the SF-86 with the Personnel Vetting Questionnaire (PVQ), with use in all vetting cases targeted for September 2027{{qpr-q3}}.

**The investigation.** In the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, initial investigations took about 57 days for Secret and 82 days for Top Secret, counting all cases. The full process, including the decision, took about 82 and 146 days{{qpr-q3}}.

**Adjudication.** An adjudicator applies the 13 guidelines in Security Executive Agent Directive 4 (SEAD 4). The review weighs the whole person, including how serious, frequent and recent any conduct was, your age at the time and evidence of rehabilitation. Any doubt is resolved in favor of national security{{sead4}}.

**Extra steps at some agencies.** Some agencies add a polygraph. A counterintelligence-scope exam covers topics such as espionage and unauthorized disclosure, and an expanded-scope exam adds criminal conduct, drug involvement and falsification{{icpg}}. The National Security Agency (NSA) also requires a psychological assessment and an interview with a clinical psychologist{{nsa-psych}}.
**Continuous vetting.** Once cleared, you are enrolled in continuous vetting, which has replaced periodic reinvestigations{{qpr-q3}}{{dcsa-cv}}.

blocks.p: Ask the hiring office whether you can start work before the final decision.

The guidelines come from SEAD 4{{sead4}}. Guideline M matters for cybersecurity students: unauthorized access to systems is a security concern even when it starts as curiosity. Practice only on platforms and systems you have permission to use.

ul: **Tell the truth.** Knowingly false statements on the form are a felony under 18 U.S.C. 1001, with up to five years in prison{{usc-1001}}{{sf86}}. Honesty falls under Guideline E{{sead4}}.

**Stop using marijuana before you apply.** Marijuana use remains a federal matter for clearances. Guidance from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) says past use is relevant but not determinative. It expects applicants to stop once they sign the SF-86, and it treats CBD products with more than 0.3% THC as marijuana{{odni-mj}}. An April 2026 rule moved only FDA-approved marijuana products and state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III{{fr-resched}}. We found no change to clearance guidance after it.
**Check agency drug rules.** Some agencies publish their own lookback periods for past drug use. The FBI's eligibility guide is one example{{fbi-elig}}.

**Keep finances current.** The SF-86 asks about debts more than 120 days delinquent and about taxes not filed or paid in the last seven years{{sf86}}. Bring any defaulted student loan back into good standing before you apply.
**Keep records as you go.** The table below lists what the SF-86 asks for{{sf86}}.

pages.title: Do research as a student
pages.metaTitle: Undergraduate and Graduate Cybersecurity Research: A Student Workflow
pages.desc: A step-by-step research workflow for cybersecurity students, from topic and literature review to quad charts, posters, papers and research ethics.
pages.summary: A research workflow from topic to paper, plus updates, posters and ethics.
pages.lede: Research shows an employer or graduate program that you can work on an open problem without an answer key. This page is the workflow we teach at CCAIR, in the order you should do it.

ol: **Topic.** Pick a problem that is new, important and tied to what stakeholders need. If no one studies it, ask why before you start.

**Domain literature.** Start with survey papers. Then read the last three to five years of top venues: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P), USENIX Security, the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS) and its AISec workshop, IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing (TDSC) and IEEE Intelligence and Security Informatics (ISI). Keep a literature matrix with one fact per cell.
**Method literature.** Find the baselines and the state of the art (NeurIPS, ICLR and KDD for machine learning). Check data fit, labels, class imbalance and interpretability.
**Gaps and research questions.** Write questions that start with how or why, never yes-or-no questions.
**Design.** Show data, method and evaluation in one diagram. Name the ground truth, the baselines and the sensitivity analyses.
**Results.** Explain why each result happened, and do not overstate it.
**Front matter last.** Write the conclusion, then the introduction, then the abstract (200 to 300 words). Keep the title near eight words, with no acronyms.

ul: **Research updates.** Put the bottom line first: your status and what you need. Number slides, caption figures, cite claims and report what failed.

**Quad chart.** One slide with four boxes: (1) objective and motivation, (2) approach and data, (3) results and impact with a metric and a baseline, (4) next steps and outputs. Use bullets, 12-point text or larger and dated milestones.
**Posters.** Put the finding in the title and build around one central figure. Use body text of 28 points or larger, and confirm the poster size with the event.
**Papers.** Turn approved slides into section headings and follow the venue's template. Read the draft aloud, then get peer review, then co-author review. Give your mentor at least a week.
**Meet on a regular schedule.** Missed meetings stall projects more than hard problems do.
**Separate brainstorming from updates.** Book a different meeting when you need to think through ideas.
**Ask about computing early.** Your mentor can tell you what campus computing is available for your project.

blocks.p: Complete your campus research ethics training before you start. If your project collects data from or about people (surveys, interviews, user logs), talk to your Institutional Review Board (IRB) before you collect it. The federal Common Rule (45 CFR 46) sets the baseline protections for human subjects research{{common-rule}}{{ohrp}}.

Security research can affect people who never agreed to take part, such as users of a network you measure. The Menlo Report sets out ethical principles for information and communication technology research{{menlo}}.

CCAIR studies the security of AI systems and the use of AI for cybersecurity. Read about [current research](/ccair/#/research) and [publications](/ccair/#/publications), then use the [contact page](/ccair/#/contact) to ask about projects. Send a resume and one paragraph on the problem you want to work on.
Need data for a project? Start with [Find data](/ccair/students/data/).

pages.title: Find data for cybersecurity projects
pages.metaTitle: Cybersecurity Datasets for Student Projects, With Known Weaknesses
pages.desc: A searchable catalog of public cybersecurity datasets for student research, with access, license, size, time span, the paper to cite and each dataset's known weaknesses.
pages.summary: A searchable catalog of datasets, each with its known weaknesses.
pages.lede: Every dataset has flaws. This catalog names them next to each entry, so you can choose data that fits your question and report its limits honestly.

ul: **Read the caveats first.** Every entry below names at least one known weakness. Report the dataset version and its weaknesses in your paper.
**Cite the paper the creators ask for.** Each entry links it.
**Check access and license terms.** Some datasets need a request or registration, and some limit commercial use.
**Get approval for data about people.** See the ethics section of [Do research](/ccair/students/research/).

sections.h: Public frameworks to pair with your data

ul: **MITRE ATT&CK.** A knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques, useful for labeling attacks{{attack}}.
**CVE.** The public list of identifiers for disclosed vulnerabilities{{cve}}.
**National Vulnerability Database (NVD).** NIST's database that adds severity scores and details to CVE records{{nvd}}.

pages.title: Scholarships and programs for cybersecurity students
pages.metaTitle: Cybersecurity Scholarships for Students: SFS, DoD and More
pages.desc: CyberCorps Scholarship for Service, the DoD Cyber Service Academy, DoD SMART, WiCyS, ISC2 scholarships and CISA internships: what each pays and who can apply.
pages.summary: CyberCorps SFS, DoD programs, WiCyS, ISC2 scholarships and CISA internships.
pages.lede: Several programs pay for a cybersecurity degree in exchange for government service, and others cover conferences or part of tuition. Amounts and deadlines change each year, so confirm them on the program's own page.

blocks.p: The National Science Foundation (NSF) funds SFS, and OPM runs the student side{{opm-sfs}}.

ul: **What it pays.** Tuition and mandatory education fees, plus an academic-year stipend of $27,000 for undergraduates and $37,000 for graduate students under the current solicitation{{nsf-sfs-sol}}.
**What you give back.** After graduation you work in a government cybersecurity or AI role for as long as the scholarship lasted{{opm-sfs}}{{nsf-sfs-sol}}.

**Who can apply.** U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents enrolled full-time at a participating school. You apply through your school, and each school runs its own selection{{opm-sfs-overview}}.
**A new name.** NSF's 2026 solicitation calls the program CyberAI SFS (CyberAICorps Scholarship for Service) and covers AI as well as cybersecurity{{nsf-sfs}}.

blocks.p: Georgia State University has an SFS program, according to the National Centers of Academic Excellence in Cybersecurity (NCAE-C) map{{cae-gsu}}.

The Department of Defense (DoD) Cyber Service Academy replaced the DoD Cyber Scholarship Program (CySP). It covers tuition, books and fees plus a stipend, in exchange for one year of DoD civilian service for each year of support. Students must be U.S. citizens enrolled at a participating NCAE-C school{{dod-csa}}.
Stipend amounts and deadlines change each cycle. Check the NCAE-C map to see whether your school takes part{{cae-map}}, then ask your campus point of contact.

The Science, Mathematics and Research for Transformation (SMART) program pays full tuition and annual stipends and includes summer internships. In return you accept one-for-one civilian service after graduation. Cybersecurity is not a listed discipline, but computer science, information sciences, software engineering and data science are. Applications open August 1{{smart}}.

WiCyS student membership costs $30 a year and needs a school-issued email address{{wicys-join}}. Members can apply for conference scholarships that cover registration and shared lodging. The round for the March 2027 conference closed September 30, 2026{{wicys-schol}}.

sections.h: ISC2 Center for Cyber Safety and Education

blocks.p: The Center awards up to $5,000 through one combined academic scholarship application for associate, undergraduate and graduate students. It asks for a GPA of 2.5 or higher, does not require U.S. citizenship and reopens in 2027{{cfcse}}.

CISA's paid student internships are posted on USAJOBS. Interns who complete 640 hours can be eligible for noncompetitive conversion to a permanent job. Applicants must be U.S. citizens, at least 16, enrolled in school, with a GPA of 2.5 or higher{{cisa-pathways}}.

ul: **Read the service terms.** Programs that pay for school usually require government service afterward. Read the agreement before you accept.
**Start a year early.** Many applications need transcripts, letters and essays.
**Ask your department.** Schools often know about local scholarships that never appear in national lists.
